title: Technical MCQ Set 08: Production Java, SQL Windows & Networking
description: Covers ExecutorService, Stream.parallel traps, SQL LAG/LEAD & OFFSET pagination, 4NF, priority inversion, CORS preflight, and Spring qualifiers.

questions.question: What does the following Java snippet print?
questions.codeSnippet:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("HCL");
System.out.println(sb.length() + ":" + sb.capacity());
questions.explanation: `new StringBuilder(String str)` allocates an internal buffer of `str.length() + 16` characters! Here `3 + 16 = 19` capacity while `length()` is `3`, printing `3:19`.

questions.question: What happens when compiling the following Java snippet?
options: Compilation error: `exception IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement`
questions.explanation: Java rejects catching a specific checked exception (other than `Exception` or `Throwable`) if no statement inside the `try` block can actually throw it.

questions.question: Determine the IEEE-754 floating-point NaN comparison result produced by this Java snippet:
questions.explanation: Unlike integer division (`0 / 0`), floating-point `0.0 / 0.0` evaluates to `Double.NaN`. Per IEEE-754, `NaN` is never equal to anything including itself (`x == x` is `false`), while `Double.isNaN(x)` returns `true`.

questions.question: How does `executor.shutdown()` differ from `executor.shutdownNow()` in Java?
options: `shutdown()` rejects new tasks while letting already submitted/queued tasks finish; `shutdownNow()` clears the pending queue and interrupts active worker threads
`shutdownNow()` blocks until every queued task completes normally
Both behave identically unless using virtual threads
questions.explanation: `shutdown()` initiates a graceful stop (finishing submitted and queued tasks); `shutdownNow()` attempts immediate cancellation by returning queued tasks and calling `interrupt()` on running workers.

questions.question: Why is calling `.parallelStream()` for blocking JDBC or HTTP I/O calls inside a high-traffic Spring Boot web server dangerous?
options: All `parallelStream()` calls share the JVM-wide `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, so blocking I/O starves unrelated parallel streams across the entire application
questions.explanation: `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` has size `CPU cores - 1`; blocking its threads on network/DB I/O stalls every other caller relying on the common pool. Use a dedicated `ExecutorService` or Java 21 virtual threads.

questions.question: If you declare `final List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();`, which operation is ILLEGAL?
questions.explanation: `final` makes the reference variable constant (cannot be reassigned to a different `ArrayList`), NOT the underlying object immutable (`add`/`clear` still mutate the list).

questions.question: Given `DailySales(dt, rev)`, which SQL expression computes each day's revenue change compared to the immediately preceding day?
questions.explanation: `LAG(rev, 1) OVER (ORDER BY dt)` fetches the prior row's `rev` ordered chronologically (`LEAD` fetches the next row).

questions.question: Why does `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` degrade on large tables and risk skipping/duplicating rows during live pagination?
options: The DB must scan and discard 100,000 rows first, and concurrent inserts shift row positions between page requests (use keyset/cursor pagination `WHERE id > last_id` instead)
`OFFSET` locks the entire table in `SERIALIZABLE` mode
questions.explanation: Offset pagination still traverses/counts `OFFSET + LIMIT` rows and suffers drift when rows are inserted/deleted; keyset pagination (`WHERE id > :cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`) stays `O(log N)` via index seek.

questions.question: Table `DevSkills(dev_id, language, certification)` stores independent multi-valued attributes (`dev_id ->> language` and `dev_id ->> certification`) in one all-key table `(dev_id, language, certification)`. Which normal form is violated?
questions.explanation: Because the table is all-key, there are no non-trivial functional dependencies (so BCNF holds), yet Cartesian repetition of two independent multi-valued facts violates 4NF.

questions.subtopic: Write Skew Anomaly in Snapshot Isolation
questions.question: Two on-call doctors check that 2 doctors are on duty, and both concurrently update their OWN distinct row to `off_call` under Snapshot Isolation, leaving 0 doctors on duty. What is this concurrency anomaly called?
options: Lost Update on the same row
questions.explanation: Write Skew occurs when two transactions read overlapping data, then update DISJOINT rows in ways that jointly violate a multi-row invariant under Snapshot Isolation (fixed by `SERIALIZABLE` or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`).

questions.question: A low-priority thread `L` holds mutex `M` needed by high-priority thread `H`, while medium-priority CPU-bound thread `M_med` continuously preempts `L`. How do real-time OS kernels resolve this Priority Inversion?
options: Priority Inheritance: temporarily boosting `L`'s priority to `H`'s priority until `L` releases mutex `M`
Converting `M` into a busy-wait spinlock on a single core
Switching the scheduler to FCFS permanently
questions.explanation: Priority Inheritance elevates the lock-holder `L` to the highest waiting thread's priority (`H`) so `M_med` cannot preempt `L` and starve `H`.

questions.question: Why does calling `fork()` followed immediately by `execve()` in a 2 GB parent process remain fast on modern Linux?
options: Copy-on-Write (CoW) shares read-only physical memory pages between parent and child, copying pages only when either writes before `execve()` replaces the address space
`fork()` copies all 2 GB sequentially to swap space
`execve()` runs inside the parent's stack frame
questions.explanation: CoW duplicates only page table entries initially marked read-only; physical pages are duplicated lazily on write faults, so `fork()+exec()` avoids copying 2 GB needlessly.

questions.question: When a React frontend on `https://app.example.com` sends a `PUT` request with `Authorization: Bearer ...` and `Content-Type: application/json` to `https://api.example.com`, what does the browser send FIRST?
options: An automatic CORS preflight `OPTIONS` request checking `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`
questions.explanation: Non-simple cross-origin requests (methods other than GET/HEAD/POST or custom headers like `Authorization` and `application/json`) trigger a browser CORS preflight `OPTIONS` check.

questions.question: In standard internet DNS resolution, which query type is sent by your laptop's stub resolver to your ISP/local recursive resolver, and which is typically used by that resolver toward Root and TLD nameservers?
options: Laptop sends iterative; resolver sends recursive to Root
Laptop sends recursive; resolver performs iterative queries (following referrals from Root -> TLD -> Authoritative)
Laptop queries Root servers directly via ARP
questions.explanation: The client asks its recursive resolver for a final answer (recursive), while Root/TLD servers return referrals (iterative) to offload state from Root infrastructure.

questions.question: While running Kahn's BFS topological sort (using vertex in-degrees) on a directed graph with `V` vertices, how do you know the graph contains a cycle?
options: At least one vertex starts with out-degree 0
The output topological list terminates with fewer than `V` vertices (remaining vertices still have `inDegree > 0`)
questions.explanation: Vertices belonging to or reachable only from a directed cycle never drop to `inDegree == 0`, so Kahn's algorithm processes strictly fewer than `V` vertices.

questions.question: Given an integer array of size `N`, what are the time complexities of a single point-update and a range-sum query `[L, R]` using a Segment Tree?
questions.explanation: A Segment Tree balances both point updates and arbitrary range queries in `O(log N)` time with `O(N)` build time and `4N` space.

questions.question: What does `statement.execute(sql)` return as its `boolean` return value?
options: `true` if at least 1 row was updated, `false` otherwise
`true` if the first result is a `ResultSet` (e.g., `SELECT`), and `false` if it is an update count or no result (e.g., `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/DDL)
`true` only if the SQL syntax is valid without running it
questions.explanation: `execute()` supports arbitrary/dynamic SQL: it returns `true` when `getResultSet()` should be called and `false` when `getUpdateCount()` applies.

questions.question: Replacing a growing `if (type.equals("UPI")) ... else if (type.equals("CARD")) ...` block with a `PaymentStrategy` interface and separate concrete implementations satisfies which SOLID principle?
options: Open-Closed Principle (open for extension, closed for modification)
questions.explanation: Adding a new payment method (`WalletPayment`) simply adds a new class implementing `PaymentStrategy` without modifying existing tested checkout code.

questions.question: Two beans `SmtpMailer` and `SesMailer` both implement `MailerService`. Without `@Primary` or `@Qualifier`, what happens when Spring Boot injects `private final MailerService mailer;`?
options: Spring picks the alphabetically first bean silently
Spring creates a dynamic proxy combining both beans
questions.explanation: When multiple candidate beans match an injection point by type and neither `@Primary` nor `@Qualifier` (nor matching field/parameter name) resolves the ambiguity, Spring throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`.

questions.subtopic: DELETE vs TRUNCATE Rollback in Transactions
questions.question: In Oracle SQL (unlike PostgreSQL), why can a `DELETE FROM Temp;` inside a transaction be undone with `ROLLBACK`, whereas `TRUNCATE TABLE Temp;` cannot?
options: In Oracle, DDL statements like `TRUNCATE` issue an implicit `COMMIT` before and after execution, preventing rollback
`DELETE` stores deleted rows inside browser cookies
questions.explanation: In Oracle (and MySQL), `TRUNCATE` is a DDL command that triggers an implicit commit, whereas PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL allowing `TRUNCATE` to roll back inside `BEGIN...ROLLBACK`.

questions.question: What is the major limitation of pure Many-to-One (user-level only) thread libraries when one user thread invokes a blocking OS `read()` syscall?
options: The OS allocates 10x more stack memory
Because the kernel sees only a single process, the blocking syscall blocks ALL user-level threads in that process and prevents multi-core parallelism
User-level threads cannot share global heap variables
Context switching between user threads requires a ring-0 kernel trap
questions.explanation: In a pure Many-to-One model, the kernel schedules only the single underlying kernel thread, so a blocking syscall stalls the entire process and cannot utilize multiple CPU cores.

questions.question: Which IPv4 address belongs to the SAME `/28` subnet as `10.0.4.37`?
A graph has `V = 100,000` vertices and `E = 250,000` edges. Why is an Adjacency List strongly preferred over an Adjacency Matrix?
options: Adjacency Matrix checks edge `(u, v)` in `O(V)` time
An Adjacency Matrix would require `10^10` cells (~10–40 GB RAM), whereas an Adjacency List uses `O(V + E)` space (~few MB)
Adjacency Lists work only on undirected trees
Adjacency Matrices cannot represent weighted edges
questions.explanation: Sparse graphs (`E << V^2`) blow up `O(V^2)` matrix memory (`10^10` entries), while an adjacency list stores only existing edges in `O(V + E)` memory.

questions.question: In Java's `Throwable` hierarchy, why should application business logic generally NOT `catch (Throwable t)` or `catch (Error e)`?
options: `Error` is a checked exception that cannot be caught
`Error` subclasses (like `OutOfMemoryError` or `StackOverflowError`) represent severe JVM/system failures that business handlers cannot reliably recover from
questions.explanation: `Error` and `Exception` both extend `Throwable` directly (`Error` is unchecked). Catching `Throwable` swallows fatal JVM `Error`s like `OutOfMemoryError` instead of letting fail-fast diagnostics surface.

questions.question: What does the following Java 8 Stream snippet print?
questions.explanation: `flatMap(Collection::stream)` flattens `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]` into a single `Stream<Integer>` of `1, 2, 3, 4`, and `sum()` returns `10`.
